text:
A suspension bridge is best understood as a system of tension where other bridges use mostly compression and bending. Its center span has very little rigid structure under the roadway by design. The deck is a relatively shallow platform, carrying the pavement, rails, vehicles, pedestrians, and sidewalks. Instead of the deck span resting on many beams all the way across, the deck acts as a light trough that gathers loads and hands them off to vertical hangers, often called suspenders. Those hangers attach along the full length of the main span and are spaced regularly. The hangers carry nearly vertical forces, which is convenient because the critical task of a suspension bridge is to turn downward deck loads into up-and-along forces in cables that cannot take compression well.

The main cables are the backbone of the bridge. They are draped as a smooth, sagging curve, close to a catenary or a parabola, over saddles near the tops of two towers. Every section of a cable has tension, and every segment of deck supported by hangers adds vertical demand along that cable. Because a hanging cable is in equilibrium, the load it carries is mostly converted into cable tension rather than into vertical bending of the cable itself. On the low, nearly flat part of the span, most of the cable’s tensile force is horizontal. Toward the towers the cable rises more steeply, so the same tension has a much larger vertical component. The accumulation of deck loads out to the halfway point is largely held by the two towers as downward forces at the cable tops, while the ends of the cables continue beyond the towers toward anchorages and transfer tension into the ground at the abutments.

This is the heart of the load path. Traffic and the weight of the deck flow downward into the roadway structure, and from there into girders, stringers, or the deck itself. The deck then passes the load laterally into closely spaced vertical suspenders. The suspenders send the load upward into the main cables. The cables carry it along their curved lengths as tension. At the towers, the vertical components of cable tension are delivered to the tower caps and saddle seats. The towers behave like slender compression columns, transferring that accumulated vertical force down their legs into foundations. The cable forces are also directed outward horizontally at the towers and toward the ends, so the bridge depends on both towers and anchorages to keep the whole geometry stable; otherwise the cable would pull the towers apart and the towers would lean outward.

The towers are therefore not merely decorative tall posts. They are the hinge-like support points that turn a long span of suspended load into compression reactions at the edges. Each tower leg is loaded largely in vertical compression, often with some bending from vibration, wind, and uneven cable pull, so it is built as a solid column or set of columns rather than a thin pole. At the bottom, the forces enter a foundation—large footings bearing on rock or dense soil, or piles driven into ground that can carry them—and are finally dispersed into the earth.

At the ends, the main cables do not simply stop at the towers. They extend to abutments and anchorages, where their tension is anchored into concrete blocks, rock, or deep foundations. This is essential. The horizontal tension in the span has to go somewhere, and in a suspension bridge it goes into the end anchorages. The towers also must resist the outward pull and the eccentric loading created by the cable directions. Stiffness, mass, shape, and foundation depth all matter because wind, earthquakes, traffic, braking forces, and thermal changes can all shift loads. Even with a good design, the bridge is not static: moving traffic redistributes suspender forces, cable sag changes, and the whole system oscillates within safe limits.

In short, a suspension bridge carries load from deck to ground by suspending the deck from tensioned cables, letting those cables sag into a self-balancing curve, delivering vertical and horizontal cable forces into towers, and driving the resulting compression through foundations into the ground. It is a chain of different structural elements—pavement, deck, hangers, cables, towers, anchorages, footings, and soil or rock—each converting the same gravitational load into a form the next element can safely resist.
